sentences.text: In this video, we'll learn coordinates on a flat map the easy way, and see how meteorology uses them to measure the winds round a hurricane's eye.
What are coordinates, and why do we need more than one kind?
This is the first of seven parts on coordinates, and in this part, we stay on a flat map.
Let's see what coordinates are, and why they're built the way they are.
Then let's see what they tell us about the winds round a hurricane.
Let's start with a flat map.
To say where something is, we need a starting point, and some directions to count from.
The starting point is called the origin.
Let's put it at a weather station.
Now draw one line through it pointing east, and one pointing north.
These lines are called the axes.
A weather balloon drifts three kilometres east and four kilometres north of the station.
So we can write its position as the pair of numbers three and four.
These two numbers are called its coordinates, and together they pin down one place on the map.
Measuring along straight axes at right angles, like this, is called Cartesian coordinates, after the French thinker René Descartes.
Each axis comes with a unit vector: an arrow of length one that points along it.
We write x hat for the arrow pointing east, and y hat for the arrow pointing north.

The balloon's position is three times x hat, plus four times y hat. Three steps of x hat take us three kilometres east, and four steps of y hat take us four kilometres north, which lands exactly on the balloon.
We met arrows like these in the vectors movie of this series.
Here's their key property: x hat points the same way everywhere on the map.
Move the balloon anywhere you like, and the two arrows don't change.
That's what makes Cartesian coordinates so easy to work with.
But many things in the weather aren't laid out in squares.
A hurricane spins round its eye, and a weather radar looks out in rings.
For those, there's a better way to say where something is.
Instead of going east and north, we can give two other numbers: how far away the balloon is, and in which direction.
The distance from the origin is called r.
By Pythagoras, r is the square root of three squared plus four squared. Three squared is nine, and four squared is sixteen, so that's the square root of twenty five: five kilometres.
The direction is an angle, called theta.
Mathematicians measure it from the east axis, turning anticlockwise as seen from above.

In a right triangle, the tangent of an angle is the side opposite it divided by the side next to it: here the north side over the east side, four over three, about one point three three. The angle with that tangent is about fifty three point one degrees, so theta is about fifty three degrees.
So the same balloon is at r equals five kilometres, and theta equals fifty three degrees.
These two numbers are called polar coordinates.
A weather radar measures exactly this pair: how far away the raindrops are, and in which direction.
Can we go back the other way?
Yes.
Think of the right triangle with the balloon at its tip.
Its long side is r, and its angle at the station is theta.
The side going east is r times cosine theta, and the side going north is r times sine theta.
Let's check.

Cosine theta is the east side divided by the long side, and sine theta is the north side divided by the long side. For our balloon that's three fifths, zero point six, and four fifths, zero point eight. So five times the cosine of theta is five times zero point six, which is three.
And five times zero point eight is four.
So x equals r cosine theta, and y equals r sine theta.
These two lines are all we need to switch between the two systems.
One warning before we go on.
Meteorologists and navigators measure directions differently.
A compass bearing starts from north, and turns clockwise as seen from above.
So the balloon's bearing is ninety minus fifty three, which is thirty seven degrees.
Weather reports add one more twist: a wind's direction says where the wind blows from, as we saw in the weather basics movie.
So a west wind blows towards the east.
Same arrows, different rulers, so it's always worth checking which angle a data set uses.
Before polar coordinates can do their real work, we need one more building block: measuring angles in radians.
Take a circle of radius r, and walk along its edge.
The angle in radians is the distance you walked, divided by the radius.
So the distance along the edge, called the arc length, is the radius times the angle.
A full circle is two pi radians, because its edge is two pi times the radius.
Two pi is about six point two eight, so one radian is three hundred and sixty degrees divided by six point two eight: about fifty seven degrees.
Let's try easy numbers.
On a ring five kilometres from the station, turn by zero point two radians: that's about eleven and a half degrees. It walks you five times zero point two, which is one kilometre.
On a ring fifty kilometres out, the same turn walks you ten kilometres.
The same angle gives ten times the distance.
Keep this rule in mind, because it explains a lot about maps of the Earth.
Polar coordinates come with their own unit vectors, so let's build them one at a time.
The first is called r hat.
It's an arrow of length one that points away from the station, towards the balloon.
Here's how to get it.
The arrow from the station to the balloon is three, four, and its length is r, five kilometres.
Dividing an arrow by its own length keeps its direction, and makes its length one.
So r hat is three fifths, four fifths, which is zero point six, zero point eight. We draw r hat at the balloon, because it tells us the direction there.
Its length is the square root of zero point six squared plus zero point eight squared. That's zero point three six plus zero point six four, which is one, and the square root of one is one.
The same works for any point.
The arrow to it is r cosine theta, r sine theta, as we just saw.
Dividing by r, the r cancels, so r hat is cosine theta, sine theta.
Why is it called r hat?
Hold theta fixed and let r grow, and the balloon slides straight outward, along this arrow.
So r hat points the way r grows.
The next few minutes build theta hat one step at a time, for anyone who enjoys seeing every move.
You don't need these steps for the intuition of weather, climate science or maps, so if it feels like too much, skip ahead to the time on screen.

So a small slide along the circle has no part along r hat: it's at right angles to r hat.
That's why the edge of a circle always runs at right angles to its radius.
But there are two directions at right angles to r hat: one turned anticlockwise from it, and one turned clockwise.

So theta hat is r hat, turned by ninety degrees anticlockwise.
To turn that picture into numbers, we need one small tool: a rule for turning any arrow by ninety degrees.

Turn y hat, which points north, and it points west.

And one last check, without using the theta hat formula.
The balloon is five kilometres from the station: three kilometres east and four north.

It moves from three thousand metres east and four thousand metres north, to about two thousand nine hundred and ninety three, and four thousand and five point two.
That's about seven metres west, and five point two metres north.
Dividing each by eight point seven gives about minus zero point eight and zero point six: theta hat again.
If you skipped, here's what to keep: r hat points away from the centre, theta hat points round it, anticlockwise, and theta hat is r hat turned by ninety degrees.
Now let's move the balloon round the circle, and watch both arrows.
Due east of the station, r hat points east, and theta hat points north.
Due north, r hat points north, and theta hat points west.
Due west, r hat points west, and theta hat points south.

That's the big difference between the two systems: polar unit vectors depend on where you are.

To sum up, coordinates are numbers that pin down a place, measured from an origin along chosen directions.
Cartesian coordinates use x and y, and their unit vectors, x hat and y hat, are the same everywhere.
Polar coordinates use the distance r and the angle theta, with x equals r cosine theta, and y equals r sine theta.

R hat points the way r grows.
